analysis.one_liner: Gave workers at larger employers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for births, adoptions, and family illness.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed the leave bill by wide margins, but President Bush vetoed it and the House override failed 258-169, so it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have entitled employees at employers with 50 or more workers to 12 weeks of unpaid leave each year for a birth, adoption, or serious illness of their own or a close family member, with their health insurance kept in force and a guaranteed return to the same or an equivalent job. It passed the Senate and House by large, partly bipartisan margins in 1991-92. President George H.W. Bush vetoed it in September 1992; the Senate voted 68-31 to override, but the House fell short of the two-thirds needed at 258-169, and the bill died.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles who had at least 12 months on the job and 1,250 hours of service — above all new parents, workers facing their own serious illness, and people caring for a sick child, spouse, or parent. The bill's own findings note that family caretaking falls disproportionately on women, so the job security mattered most to them [S4][S7]. Federal civil-service employees, and eventually the Senate's and House's own staff, were covered as well [S5][S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: New parents and seriously ill workers

how_it_helps.text: Gave eligible workers 12 workweeks of leave in any 12-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, their own serious health condition, or care of a child, spouse, or parent with a serious health condition.
Required the employer to restore the worker to the same or an equivalent position with equal pay and benefits, and to keep group health coverage in force during the leave.

Made the rights enforceable: the Secretary of Labor could investigate and act on complaints, and workers could sue in court, with liquidated damages and attorney's fees available against employers who deny leave or retaliate.
Covered federal civil-service employees under parallel rules, and the final version applied the same protections to Senate and House employees — Congress put its own staff under the law.

Congress's stated findings were that workers were being forced to choose between job security and parenting, and that the burden of family caretaking falls mainly on women, which the gender-neutral leave entitlement was meant to ease.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — businesses and public agencies with 50 or more employees. They would have had to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, keep paying the employee's group health insurance premiums during unpaid leave, arrange temporary replacements, and administer certification and notice rules [S4][S7]. The bill was designed to limit the cost: the leave itself was unpaid, employers could require workers to substitute accrued paid vacation or sick leave, and employers with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles were exempt [S2][S4].

drawbacks.text: The leave was unpaid. Employers were expressly not required to provide any paid sick or medical leave they did not already offer, so many workers could not afford to take the 12 weeks the bill guaranteed.

Eligibility was narrow: workers needed 12 months on the job and 1,250 hours of service in the prior year, and any employer with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles of the worksite was entirely exempt.
Married couples employed by the same employer had to share a single 12-week entitlement for a birth, adoption, or care of a sick parent.
Employers could deny reinstatement to the highest-paid 10 percent of their local workforce if returning them would cause 'substantial and grievous economic injury' to operations.

Employers gained litigation exposure: workers could sue for lost wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, plus attorney's fees, which business groups in the minority views and the Bush Labor Department's unfavorable comment flagged as a burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers was real but modest: job security, not income, during life's hardest moments, since the leave was unpaid and roughly a third or more of the workforce fell outside coverage by design. The cost to employers was limited by the same design — unpaid leave, paid-leave substitution, the 50-employee threshold, and special rules for schools — leaving mainly replacement costs, health-premium maintenance during leave, and litigation exposure. A fair reading is that the bill bought meaningful job protection at a deliberately contained cost, and the strongest objection is that the protection was hollow for workers without savings to fund an unpaid 12 weeks.

outcome.mechanism: President George H.W. Bush vetoed the bill after both chambers passed it; the Senate voted 68-31 to override, but the House override fell short of the needed two-thirds at 258-169, so the bill died.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on January 14, 1991, with a long bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Kennedy, Packwood, D'Amato, Jeffords, and Hatfield.

The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee held hearings and reported the bill in May 1991 with a substitute amendment and minority views filed; the Labor Department submitted an unfavorable executive comment.
The Senate passed the bill by voice vote on October 2, 1991, and the House passed it without objection on November 13, 1991, inserting the text of its companion measure, H.R. 2.

A conference committee filed its report on August 10, 1992; the Senate agreed to it by unanimous consent the next day, and the House adopted it 241-161 on September 10, 1992, with 203 of 267 Democrats and 37 of 166 Republicans in favor.
President Bush vetoed the bill on September 22, 1992, citing among other things the mandate it placed on employers.

The Senate overrode the veto 68-31 on September 24, with 54 of 57 Democrats and 14 of 43 Republicans in favor. On September 30 the House override reached 258-169 — short of the two-thirds required — and the veto was sustained.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers were better off: they avoided a 12-week job-protected leave mandate, the requirement to keep paying health premiums during leave, and the damages-and-fees liability that came with it. Working families got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared the leave mandate; families got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed with real bipartisan support — the Senate overrode 68-31 with 14 of 43 Republicans joining, and 37-38 House Republicans backed it — but opposition concentrated among Republicans: 127 of 166 House Republicans and 28 of 43 Senate Republicans voted to sustain the veto, while Democrats backed it 54-3 and 219-42.

industries.industry: Employers with 50 or more employees (businesses and public agencies)
industries.note: The bill mandated 12 weeks of job-protected leave, continued health coverage during unpaid leave, and created damages-and-attorney's-fees liability for interference. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the workers the bill covered, and its allies in Congress and the White House kept the mandate from taking effect.

industries.industry: Small employers (fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles)
industries.note: They were exempted from coverage, avoiding costs larger rivals had to bear, though their employees received no federal leave protection. A commission was set up to study whether to cover smaller businesses later.

industries.industry: Local educational agencies and private schools
industries.note: Covered, but with special rules letting schools require teachers to take leave in defined blocks or transfer positions near the end of academic terms, and a path to reduced liability.
